title: Topological and kinetic origins of fractional thermal conductance at the topological insulator--superconductor interface
authors: Laurence A. Jacobs, Guillermo R. Zemba
abstract: A recent experiment by Roy et al. (Nat. Commun. 17, 2853 (2026)) demonstrated a robust half-integer thermal conductance plateau, κ_0 T/2, at a bipolar (ν,ν')=(2,-1) junction in bilayer graphene, produced not by non-Abelian topology but by full equilibration of co-propagating electron and hole edge modes. We prove a theorem that fixes when the two origins can be told apart: under full thermal equilibration, the two-terminal thermal conductance of a network of chiral edge segments joined at ideal floating contacts is a rational function of the net chiral central charges of the segments alone, quantities pinned by the gravitational anomaly and invariant under arbitrary local boundary kinetics. The corollary is an impossibility statement: whenever two realizations present the same anomaly data to the same network, no thermal-conductance measurement can distinguish them. That the equilibrated (2,-1) value equals the central charge of a chiral Majorana mode is an arithmetic fact about one filling combination, but wherever such a coincidence occurs it is beyond the reach of thermometry, and the separation must come from the charge sector, which is not anomaly-pinned at a superconducting boundary. We develop the topological insulator-superconductor interface as the application: a vortex carries fractional charge e/4 from the θ= πmagnetoelectric coupling, the boundary hosts a chiral Majorana mode of central charge 1/2, and a laterally adjacent integer quantum Hall (IQH) region supplies the kinetic realization. The Lorenz ratio (anomalous for the isolated Majorana boundary, L_0 / (1 + 4|ν_{IQH}|) in the composite device) and the excess shot noise (growing with B from e/4 vortex tunneling versus locked to IQH plateaus) together resolve the mechanism, provided the quantum Hall edge does not abut the superconductor.
summary: This theoretical work establishes that thermal conductance alone cannot distinguish between topological and kinetic origins of fractional conductance in edge systems. The authors prove that the separation requires analyzing the charge sector, specifically using the Lorenz ratio and shot noise measurements, which are sensitive to the underlying charge dynamics at the superconducting boundary.
main_problem: The paper addresses the fundamental challenge of distinguishing between fractional thermal conductance arising from non-Abelian topology (like Majorana modes) versus that arising from full thermal equilibration of co-propagating edge modes.
main_result: A theorem proves that under full thermal equilibration, the thermal conductance ($\kappa_{th}$) depends only on the net chiral central charges, making it impossible to distinguish the two origins using $\kappa_{th}$ alone. Separation requires analyzing the charge sector via the Lorenz ratio and shot noise.
method: The analysis uses boundary Conformal Field Theory (CFT) to derive universal formulas for energy currents and thermal conductance, followed by applying energy conservation principles to composite quantum systems.
model_or_system: The primary theoretical model is a network of chiral edge segments joined at ideal floating contacts, applied specifically to the topological insulator–superconductor (TI–SC) interface involving Majorana and Integer Quantum Hall (IQH) edge modes.
key_observables: Thermal conductance ($\kappa_{th}$), Lorenz ratio ($\mathcal{L}$), and excess shot noise (Fano factor).
important_parameters: Net chiral central charges ($c_i$), temperature ($T$), and magnetic field ($B$).
main_assumptions: The theorem relies on the assumption of full thermal equilibration and ideal floating contacts; the separation mechanism requires the IQH edge not to abut the superconductor.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the general setup for the anomaly-pinned theorem using chiral edge segments; Figure 2 (mentioned) shows the geometry for explicit three-segment calculations.
paper_structure: The paper first proves the general Anomaly Pinning Theorem for thermal conductance in edge networks (Section II), then applies this to the TI–SC interface (Section III/IV), concluding that charge-sector diagnostics (Lorenz ratio, noise) are necessary for resolution (Section V).
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous theoretical framework for diagnosing the microscopic origin of quantized transport phenomena in topological materials, suggesting that electrical measurements (charge sector) are necessary when thermal measurements (energy sector) fail to distinguish mechanisms.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: FIG. 1. The setting of Theorem 1. Chiral edge segments of net central charge ci = cR,i −cL,i, each long compared with its thermal equilibration length, joined at ideal floating contacts, measured between two reservoirs at ua = T 2 a and ub = T 2 b . The connectivity is arbitrary; the three-segment chain of Fig. 2 is one case. The two hypotheses and the conclusion are the three panels: everything microscopic about a segment enters only through ci, and the rational function R is fixed by the connectivity alone.

FIG. 2. The three-segment series geometry realized by the device of Roy et al. and by the platform of Sec. IV B. Lemma 1 at each floating contact makes the heat current common to the three segments, and eliminating the interior temperatures gives the series law. When the two outer segments are identical the coefficient is (9): the factor 2 in the Roy formula (1) is the multiplicity with which the outer phase is traversed, not a branching of the circuit.

FIG. 3. The TI–SC interface. A perpendicular field threads the interface and generates an Abrikosov lattice of singly quantized vortices; each carries a Fu–Kane Majorana zero mode at its core and, from the θ = π magnetoelectric coupling, the polarization charge (13). The chain below records the origin of the e/4: the half-quantized surface Hall conductance of the θ = π surface, multiplied by the superconducting flux quantum Φ0 = h/2e. The boundary of the region carries a chiral Majorana mode of central charge cM = 1

FIG. 4. Three candidate devices, and why the choice is not cosmetic. (A) A line junction: the quantum-Hall layer is laterally adjacent and separated from the superconductor by a normal or insulating spacer, so its charged modes survive and G = |νIQH|e2/h. This is the geometry adopted, and the object treated by the line-junction kinetic theory of Refs. [20, 21]. (B) Everything on one TI surface, where central charges attach to domain walls rather than regions: SC | magnetic walls carry 2n + 1 chiral Majoranas, c = n + 1
